body: **Summary:** FMCG companies sell branded, frequently purchased goods through a distribution network that reaches ~8–10 million outlets. Profit comes from brand-led pricing power, gross margin over commodities (palm oil, crude derivatives, milk, wheat, cocoa) and scale in advertising and distribution. Negative working capital and asset-light models drive RoCE of 50–100%+. Key metrics: underlying volume growth (UVG), price/mix growth, gross margin, EBITDA margin, A&P % of sales, rural against urban growth, distribution reach (direct outlets), market share (NielsenIQ), and channel mix (modern trade, e-commerce, quick commerce). Cycle drivers: rural income (monsoon, MSP, rural wages), food inflation (which squeezes discretionary spend), commodity cycles, GST changes (Sep 2025 rate rationalisation), competition from D2C and regional brands, and quick commerce. Lead indicators: NielsenIQ quarterly FMCG volume tracker, rural wage data (Labour Bureau), MGNREGA demand, IMD monsoon, CPI food, tractor and 2W sales as rural proxies. Winners (HUL, Nestle, Britannia over 2000–2020) kept volume-led growth, category creation, premiumisation and distribution depth. Losers were companies that relied on price-led growth, failed to adapt to new channels or made diversification bets. Valuation: P/E 40–60x for leaders. The peak came in 2019–21, and multiples have since compressed as growth slowed. FMCG P/E was 33.8 in Jun 2026 against a 7-year median of 41.8. Nov 2026: Q2 FY27 FMCG value growth was a six-quarter high of 8.6%, with rural at 10.6% against urban at 5.8%, and HUL UVG ~7%. Traps: paying 60x for 4% volume growth, and pricing-led quarters. Sources: [1](https://www.sahi.com/news/india-fmcg-value-growth-hits-six-quarter-high-of-8-6-in-q2fy27-on-rural-surge) · [2](https://ticker.finology.in/discover/market-update/hul-q2-fy27-results-analysis) · [3](https://www.indexpe.in/blog/nifty-sector-valuations-june-2026) Links: about `insight:myth-titan-3`

body:
`insight:india-mb-twin-engine-base-rate` · confidence: verified

Decomposition of 27 Indian winner windows (25 case records plus BEL and both shipyards; screener TTM P/E, split-adjusted prices): log(price multiple) = log(EPS multiple) + log(P/E multiple). Median share of the log-return from rerating = 37%. Long runs (9+ years: Bajaj Finance, Page, Astral, Pidilite, Titan, Eicher, Balkrishna, APL Apollo, Deepak, Tata Elxsi, Garware, Alkyl) had a median rerating share of ~36%; EPS compounding did most of the work. Short runs (≤5.5 years: KPIT 62%, Cochin 88%, HAL 66%, Mazagon 53%, CDSL 50%, Dixon 42%, Kaynes 29%, Trent 14%) had a median of ~51%. Rerating-heavy cases (>50% from P/E: Cochin, HAL, KPIT, Symphony, Balkrishna, Tata Elxsi, Mazagon, CDSL) are a median ~54% below their ATH on 19 Nov 2026. HAL (−14%), whose EPS kept rising, is the exception. Earnings-heavy cases (≤30%: Trent, Page, Titan, Avanti, Eicher, Caplin, La Opala, Polycab, Kaynes) had mixed outcomes: Titan and Eicher are near highs, while La Opala and Kaynes are down 60%+. Where they fell, it was because growth slowed, not because a pure multiple was undone. Rule: when more than half of a gain is multiple, the gain is fragile; check whether EPS can carry the price if P/E returns to its median. Caveat: windows start at lows, which inflates P/E expansion.

body:
Unit of record = one **promise** (memdb `type: promise`), extracted from each concall, investor presentation, annual report MD&A, chairman's letter or press release.

```json
{
  "type": "promise",
  "id": "promise:KPITTECH-2026Q2-ebitda-margin-20pct",
  "tickers": ["KPITTECH"],
  "title": "EBITDA margin back to ~20-21% by early CY2027",
  "date": "2026-10-28",
  "data": {
    "source_doc": "Q2FY27 concall transcript", "source_url": "https://nsearchives.nseindia.in/corporate/KPITTECH_03112026220723_KPIT_Q2FY27_Transcript_Signed.pdf",
    "speaker": "Kishor Patil (CEO)", "quote": "it will go up to some extent, every quarter, but, it will be early next year when we get there",
    "category": "margin",            // revenue_growth | margin | capex | capacity_commissioning | order_inflow | order_book | debt_reduction | working_capital | new_product | approval_regulatory | customer_win | m&a | dividend_payout | other
    "metric": "EBITDA margin %", "baseline": null, "target_low": 20, "target_high": 21, "unit": "%",
    "deadline": "2027-03-31", "deadline_precision": "half-year",   // exact-date | quarter | half-year | fiscal-year | vague
    "specificity": 2,                // 0 vague aspiration .. 3 number+date+metric
    "unprompted": false,             // volunteered in opening remarks vs extracted by analyst question
    "conditionality": "growth accelerating in H2",
    "status": "open",                // open | delivered | partially_delivered | missed | moved_goalpost | withdrawn | superseded
    "status_history": [{"as_of":"2026-10-28","status":"open","evidence":"stated"}],
    "check_after": ["Q3FY27 results", "Q4FY27 results"],
    "resolution": null, "resolved_on": null, "delivery_ratio": null   // actual / promised
  }
}
```

**What to extract from each call.** Run an LLM pass with a fixed prompt, then a human spot-check.
1. Revenue/volume growth guidance (FY, multi-year CAGR), by segment.
2. Margin targets (EBITDA, gross, segment) and the stated drivers.
3. Capex: amount, use, **commissioning date**, peak-revenue potential, asset turn claimed.
4. Order inflow/book: targets, book-to-bill, the pipeline figure quoted, L1 positions.
5. Balance sheet: debt reduction targets, working-capital days, receivable resolution, promoter pledge release.
6. Product/approval timelines: USFDA approvals, launches, customer qualifications, PLI disbursement.
7. Capital allocation: dividend policy, buyback, M&A, fundraising.
8. **Explanations** of last quarter's miss (to test later whether the "one-off" really was one-off).
9. Things management **stopped mentioning**. Diff the topic list against prior calls, Lazy Prices style. A KPI dropped from the presentation is a strong signal.

body:
- **Top-down.** FY26 plan: "approximately $100 million of our cash capital expenditure budget … to construct and open approximately 150 net new stores". The plan "exclude[s] the impact of tenant allowances" `[10K25 Item 7]`. That is **~$0.65M gross build-out per store** (≈155 gross openings).
- **Bottom-up of the company's $0.4M:**
  - build-out net of tenant allowances = X;
  - inventory net of payables ≈ $0.14M [EST: store inventory ~$250k × (1 − AP/inventory 43%)];
  - pre-opening ≈ $0.094M [$14.8M ÷ 157 openings `[10K25 n.1(t)]`].
  - So X ≈ $0.17M, which needs **tenant allowances of ~$0.48M per store (~74% of build-out).** That is implausible for a 9,500 sq ft strip-centre box. A 20–35% allowance is the usual range [benchmark, unverified].
- **If tenant allowances are ~$0.15–0.25M, the true cash investment is ~$0.6–0.7M,** and the payback is ~1.6–1.9 years at $370k. That is still excellent retail economics, but **50–75% longer than the headline**.
- **Network capex outside the model:** five ship centres cost ~$270M to buy, build or expand (Forsyth $42M + $21M, Conroe $56M, Buckeye $65M + $26M, Indianapolis $60M) `[10K25 Item 2]` and serve ~1,900 stores. That is **~$0.14M per store of DC capex**, plus systems (ERP, HCM).
- **The gap is the finding** (rule from technique #1, ">30% gap"). Questions for IR or the next transcript: (a) the average tenant allowance per new store; (b) whether the $0.4M is a current-cohort figure or legacy text; (c) the FY24 and FY25 cohort's first-year sales against $2M. Management says "new store productivity again outperformed" `[CC-Q2FY26]`. That is a comparison with their own model, not a number.
